t.3.34.1: Mārīca, dear friend, let the words I speak be heard. I am in distress, and to me in my distress you are indeed the highest refuge.
t.3.34.2: You know Janasthāna, where my brother Khara dwells, and the mighty-armed Dūṣaṇa, and my sister Śūrpaṇakhā too.
t.3.34.3: And Triśiras, the mighty rākṣasa of great splendour, eater of flesh, and many other heroic night-rangers who had attained their aim in battle.
t.3.34.4: Those rākṣasas who, by my command, dwell in their settlement in the great forest, harassing the sages who practise dharma.
t.3.34.5: Fourteen thousand rākṣasas of terrible deeds, valiant warriors who never missed their mark and who followed the will of Khara…
t.3.34.6: But those mighty ones, who were then dwelling in Janasthāna, fully prepared and intent, met Rāma in battle.
t.3.34.7: Thereupon, at the forefront of the battle, Rāma, whose anger had been roused, without uttering a single harsh word, set his bow to work with arrows.
t.3.34.8: Fourteen thousand rākṣasas of dreadful deeds have been slain with sharp arrows by a mere man fighting on foot.
t.3.34.9: Khara has been slain in battle, and Dūṣaṇa has been struck down; and having killed Triśiras as well, he has made the Daṇḍaka forests free from fear.
t.3.34.11: He is devoid of good conduct, harsh, fierce, foolish and greedy, with his senses unconquered; having abandoned dharma, he is wicked at heart and delights in harming living beings.
t.3.34.10: Banished by his angry father and accompanied by his wife, his life already waning, he is the slayer of that army: Rāma, the disgrace of the kṣatriyas.
t.3.34.12: He by whom, in the forest, without any cause for enmity, relying solely on his strength, my sister was disfigured through the cutting off of her ears and nose.
t.3.34.13: By force I shall carry off from Janasthāna his wife Sītā, who is like a daughter of the gods; be my helper in that.
t.3.34.14: For with you as my companion standing at my side, O mighty one, and with my brothers, I give no thought to all the gods together in battle.
t.3.34.15: Therefore, be my helper, for you are capable, O Rākṣasa; in valor, in battle, and in pride there is none equal to you.
t.3.34.16: For this purpose I have come to you, O night-wanderer. Hear the task that must be done, at my word, by way of help to me.
t.3.34.17: Becoming a golden deer, dappled with spots of silver, wander in that Rāma's hermitage, in front of Sītā.
t.3.34.18: But without a doubt, Sītā, on seeing you in the form of a deer, will say to her husband and to Lakṣmaṇa, "Let it be caught!"
t.3.34.19: Then, when those two have gone away and the place is deserted, I shall carry off Sītā at my ease, unhindered, as Rāhu seizes the radiance of the moon.
t.3.34.20: Then afterwards, when Rāma is worn down by the abduction of his wife, I shall strike at him with ease and without fear, my inner self having achieved its aim.
t.3.34.21: Hearing from him that talk of Rāma, the great-souled Mārīca's mouth went dry, and he became utterly terrified.
t.3.34.22: He, his mind frightened and dejected, knowing well Rāma's prowess in the great forest, joined his palms and spoke to Rāvaṇa words that were true, beneficial to him and beneficial to himself as well.
